# Project 2: Victoria Park FastSLAM {#sec-project2}

Around the turn of the millennium, researchers at the Australian Centre for Field Robotics drove a utility vehicle around Victoria Park in Sydney for 26 minutes and about 4 km, logging wheel speed, steering angle, a GPS receiver that was quietly failing, and a SICK laser scanner sweeping 180 degrees in front of the bumper [@VictoriaParkDataset]. The park is full of trees, and to a laser a tree trunk is a small, round, isolated return: a natural landmark, the way a lighthouse or a charted headland is for a coastal navigator. A quarter of a century later the log is still one of the standard tests for landmark SLAM, because it is real, it is messy, and it punishes every shortcut.

``` text
laser scan (361 ranges) --> tree extractor (Part A) --> z = (r, beta) per trunk
                                                            |
odometry 40 Hz (v_e, delta) --> encoder correction + lever arm (Part A)
                                                            |
                event-driven time sync --> FastSLAM 1.0 (Parts B and C)
                                                            |
            laser track + tree map --> SE(2)-aligned error vs GPS (Part D)
```

Project 2 builds that pipeline. Much of the work is not the famous algorithm, which you have already seen running in @sec-slam. It is the part every navigation engineer spends their career on: knowing where each sensor is on the vehicle and what its numbers mean (a speed measured on one wheel, a laser 3.8 m in front of the axle the kinematics are written about, bearings measured from the vehicle's right-hand side), and lining up sensors that never sample at the same instant. Get those wrong and no number of particles will save you.

## Overview {#sec-project2-overview}

You will implement **FastSLAM 1.0** for the Victoria Park dataset: vehicle poses are particles sampled from the motion model, and each particle carries its own map of tree landmarks, one tiny EKF per tree [@Montemerlo2002FastSLAM; @Thrun2004FastSLAM]. FastSLAM 2.0 is an optional extension once a working FastSLAM 1.0 baseline exists. The project is worth **25% of the course grade**.

**Learning outcomes.** By the end of the project you should be able to

- decode a real sensor log, including its bit-packed fields and undocumented corners, and verify each convention against the data rather than trusting the documentation;
- model a vehicle whose speed sensor, steering geometry, and exteroceptive sensor sit at different places, and carry the lever arm consistently through the motion and observation models;
- synchronize a 40 Hz control stream with an irregular, slower measurement stream without smearing the measurements;
- extract repeatable point landmarks from 2D laser scans and characterize the extractor's errors;
- implement per-particle data association with two statistical gates, landmark birth and deletion, and correctly weighted particles;
- evaluate a SLAM solution honestly against an imperfect reference, and explain its failure modes and sensitivities.

You may adapt any of it, with attribution: cite the section in a code comment and in the report. ## Dataset {#sec-project2-dataset}

Download the Victoria Park data once from the repository root:

``` bash
uv run python scripts/fetch_data.py victoria-park
```

This places the original files in `data/victoria-park/`:

``` text
data/victoria-park/
  aa3_lsr2.mat       # LASER (7249 x 361 uint16), TLsr (ms)
  aa3_dr.mat         # speed (m/s), steering (rad), time (ms): 61945 samples
  aa3_gpsx.mat       # Lo_m, La_m (m), timeGps (ms): 4466 fixes
  info.txt, car.bmp  # sensor conventions and the vehicle drawing
  detectTreesI16.m   # the original ACFR tree detector (MATLAB)
  viewLsr.m          # the original scan viewer (shows the laser decoding)
```

The starter tools find `data/victoria-park` automatically. If you keep a copy elsewhere, pass that directory explicitly or set the `ADVNAV_DATA_DIR` environment variable to the folder that contains `victoria-park/`.

The facts below are the ones that bite. Each was checked on the data; the reasoning is in @sec-mapping-vehicle-model and @sec-mapping-laser-conventions.

| Quantity | What the log contains | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Laser ranges | `uint16` words: low 13 bits = range in cm, top 3 bits = flags | `raw & 0x1FFF`, divide by 100; values $\ge$ 8000 cm mean "no return" (about 83% of all beams) |
| Laser angles | 361 beams, scanner angle $A = 0, 0.5, \ldots, 180$ degrees, $A = 0$ to the vehicle's **right** | bearing in the vehicle frame $\beta = A - \pi/2$ (positive to the left) |
| Laser timing | a scan every 213-215 ms; the first scan (21.819 s) precedes the first odometry sample (21.940 s) | see @sec-project2-time-synchronization |
| Speed | measured by an encoder on the **rear-left** wheel | convert to centerline speed (@eq-project2-encoder) |
| Steering | front-wheel angle, positive = left turn, 40 Hz | |
| Laser position | 3.78 m ahead of the rear axle, 0.50 m to the left | lever arm in the motion model (@eq-project2-laser-kinematics) |
| GPS | antenna at the laser; ~5 Hz; gaps up to 58 s; dozens of jumps; local east/north frame | reference only, never a filter measurement; compare only after SE(2) alignment (@sec-project2-evaluation-protocol) |

`load_victoria_park_data()` applies the decoding and unit conversions, keeps the raw words in `dataset.laser_raw`, and exposes GPS as `dataset.gps_xy_m` (`[Lo_m, La_m]` = east, north). GPS is useful for plots, sanity checks, and the final evaluation. It must not enter the filter.

What you write, with the signatures the tests and `run_all` call:

``` python
extract_tree_landmarks(scan_ranges_m, *, pose_guess=None)        # -> list[TreeObservation]
LandmarkEKF.initialize(pose, measurement, measurement_covariance, *, time_s=0.0)
landmark.innovation(pose, measurement, measurement_covariance)   # -> (nu, H_l, S)
landmark.updated(pose, measurement, measurement_covariance, *, time_s=None)   # -> new LandmarkEKF
slam.predict(speed_mps, steering_rad, dt_s)
slam.associate(particle, measurements)                           # -> list[Association]
slam.update(observations, time_s)
slam.resample()
```

Their docstrings are the detailed contract. Keep those signatures stable; add helpers, keyword-only options, and modules freely. Note that `landmark.updated(...)` returns a *new* landmark and leaves the old one alone: after resampling, several particles share the same landmark objects (`particle.copy()` copies the dictionary, not the landmarks), which is what makes resampling cheap (@sec-slam-why-fast). Mutating a shared landmark in place silently edits other particles' maps.

The tests of your deliverables skip with a "not implemented yet" message until you write the corresponding method, then start checking it, so `uv run pytest projects/victoria_park_slam` is a quick sanity check as you go. They check interfaces and simple cases (a synthetic scan with two trunks and a wall, the two gates, a loop through a synthetic forest), not whether your Victoria Park solution is good. `uv run python -m victoria_park_slam.run_all` runs whatever you have implemented on the first 2000 scans and reports the rest as not implemented. Its `TUNING` block is where your values go.

## System Model {#sec-project2-system-model}

The filter state of particle $i$ is the **laser pose**

$$
\mathbf{x}^{[i]} =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_L & y_L & \theta
\end{bmatrix}^T,
$$

the world position of the laser (which is also where the GPS antenna is) and the vehicle heading $\theta$, counter-clockwise from the world $x$ axis. Writing the state at the laser, rather than at the rear axle the kinematics are naturally written about, keeps the observation model a plain range-bearing model and makes the estimate directly comparable to GPS. The price is paid once, in the motion model.

The map is a set of 2D tree positions, $\{\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\ell}_N\}$ with $\boldsymbol{\ell}_j = [\ell_{x,j}, \ell_{y,j}]^T$, each with its own $2\times2$ covariance $\mathbf{P}_{\ell,j}$ inside each particle. The controls are the logged encoder speed and steering angle, $\mathbf{u} = [v_e, \delta]^T$, and one observation is the range and vehicle-frame bearing of a trunk center, $\mathbf{z} = [r, \beta]^T$. Your front end may also estimate trunk diameters, but the FastSLAM update uses only $\mathbf{z}$.

## Vehicle Model and Lever Arm {#sec-project2-forward-mechanization-state}

@sec-mapping-vehicle-model derives the geometry; here is what you implement. The vehicle (drawing in `car.bmp`, numbers in `info.txt`) has wheelbase $L = 2.83$ m. Its speed encoder sits on the rear-left wheel, $H = 0.76$ m left of the centerline, so in a left turn it rolls on a tighter circle than the axle center and reads low. The centerline speed is

$$
v_c = \frac{v_e}{1 - \dfrac{H}{L}\tan\delta}.
$$ {#eq-project2-encoder}

The laser is $a = L + 0.95 = 3.78$ m ahead of the rear axle and $b = 0.50$ m to the left of the centerline. (The drawing labels the 0.95 m front-axle-to-laser distance $a$; kinematic models need the distance from the rear axle.) With $\omega = (v_c/L)\tan\delta$, the laser moves as Guivant and Nebot's laser-centered kinematics say [@GuivantNebot2001CompressedEKFSLAM]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot x_L &= v_c\cos\theta - \omega\,(a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta),\\
\dot y_L &= v_c\sin\theta + \omega\,(a\cos\theta - b\sin\theta),\\
\dot\theta &= \omega.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-project2-laser-kinematics}

The extra terms are the lever arm: when the vehicle yaws, a point 3.8 m in front of the rear axle swings sideways at $\omega a$, a meter per second in a brisk turn. For controls held constant over a step, `predict_laser_pose(laser_pose, centerline_speed_mps, steering_rad, dt_s, geometry)` integrates @eq-project2-laser-kinematics exactly: it moves the pose back along the lever arm to the rear axle, follows the bicycle arc, and moves out again. `encoder_to_centerline_speed` implements @eq-project2-encoder. Both are vectorized over particles.

These corrections are not cosmetic. Over the first 200 s, dead reckoning aligned to GPS has an RMSE of 28 m without the encoder correction and 13 m with it. The lever arm hardly changes that number, because GPS noise hides a half-meter effect, but it visibly sharpens the map in turns; Part A asks you to show both.

**Process noise.** FastSLAM 1.0 samples each particle from the motion model by perturbing the measured controls,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{[i]} &= \begin{bmatrix} v_e \\ \delta \end{bmatrix} + \boldsymbol{\eta}^{[i]},\\
\boldsymbol{\eta}^{[i]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_u),
\end{aligned}
$$

and propagating with the noisy controls, encoder correction included. `MotionModelConfig.control_noise_covariance` is $\mathbf{Q}_u$, drawn once per `predict` call. Read the warning in @sec-project2-time-synchronization before you tune it.

## Time Synchronization {#sec-project2-time-synchronization}

Odometry arrives every 25 ms and laser scans every 213-215 ms, on the same clock but never at the same instant. Grabbing "the nearest odometry sample" for a scan, or integrating one big step per scan, places every observation at the wrong pose: at 6 m/s a 25 ms error is 15 cm along track, and in a turn the heading error moves a tree 40 m away by another 30 cm. The fix is an event-driven merge:

1. treat odometry sample $k$, logged at $t_k$, as a zero-order hold over $[t_k, t_{k+1})$;
2. between two scans, call `predict` once for each odometry interval;
3. split the last interval at the laser timestamp: predict up to the scan, update, then predict the rest of the interval before the next scan.

`scan_steps(dataset)` yields, for every scan, the pieces to propagate (`step.controls`, each a `(speed_mps, steering_rad, dt_s)` record) and the update time `step.time_s`; `run_all` drives your filter with it:

``` python
for step in scan_steps(dataset, 0, 2000):
    for control in step.controls:
        slam.predict(control.speed_mps, control.steering_rad, control.dt_s)
    slam.update(extract_tree_landmarks(dataset.laser_ranges_m[step.scan_index]), step.time_s)
```

The very first scan (21.819 s) precedes the first odometry sample (21.940 s), so nothing is known about the motion before it; `scan_steps` skips it. You may use the helper or write your own merge, but your report must explain the timing model either way.

**Tune $\mathbf{Q}_u$ to the step rate.** Each `predict` call draws fresh, independent noise, so control noise is sampled at 40 Hz. Independent errors average out: with per-step steering noise $\sigma_\delta$, the heading spread after $T$ seconds grows like

$$
\sigma_\theta(T) \approx \frac{v}{L}\,\sigma_\delta\,\sqrt{T\,\Delta t},
$$

which for $v = 4$ m/s, $\sigma_\delta = 3^\circ$, and $\Delta t = 25$ ms is under a degree after a full second. Real odometry errors (a steering offset, tire slip, a scale error) are correlated over seconds, so a $\mathbf{Q}_u$ that looks physically reasonable per sample is far too small, and an overconfident particle cloud loses track exactly where it matters. If you change the step rate (sub-stepping, or one prediction per scan), rescale $\mathbf{Q}_u$; the pose spread over a fixed time scales like $\mathbf{Q}_u\,\Delta t$.

## Observation Model {#sec-project2-observation-model}

With the laser pose as the state, a trunk at $\boldsymbol{\ell}_j$ is observed at

$$
h(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j) =
\begin{bmatrix}
\sqrt{q} \\
\operatorname{wrap}\!\left(\operatorname{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x) - \theta\right)
\end{bmatrix},
$$

with $\Delta x = \ell_{x,j} - x_L$, $\Delta y = \ell_{y,j} - y_L$, and $q = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2$. The measurement is $\mathbf{z} = h(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j) + \mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R})$. The bearing is in the vehicle frame, $\beta = A - \pi/2$ (@sec-mapping-laser-conventions); a trunk on the left has a positive bearing. Inside one particle the pose is treated as known, so the landmark EKF needs only the Jacobian with respect to the landmark,

$$
\mathbf{H}_\ell =
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta x/\sqrt{q} & \Delta y/\sqrt{q} \\
-\Delta y/q & \Delta x/q
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

A new landmark comes from the inverse model,

$$
\boldsymbol{\ell} =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_L + r\cos(\theta + \beta) \\
y_L + r\sin(\theta + \beta)
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and its covariance from the Jacobian $\mathbf{G}_z$ of that model with respect to the measurement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{G}_z &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(\theta+\beta) & -r\sin(\theta+\beta) \\
\sin(\theta+\beta) & r\cos(\theta+\beta)
\end{bmatrix},\\
\mathbf{P}_\ell &= \mathbf{G}_z\mathbf{R}\mathbf{G}_z^T.
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathbf{G}_z = \mathbf{H}_\ell^{-1}$ at the same point, a useful check. `range_bearing_prediction`, `range_bearing_jacobian`, `inverse_range_bearing`, and `inverse_range_bearing_jacobian` implement these, and `numerical_jacobian` lets you verify any Jacobian you add (the tests do exactly that). If you prefer a rear-axle state, the lever arm moves into $h$ and its Jacobians; that is allowed, but derive and test it, and keep the evaluation at the laser.

## FastSLAM Specification {#sec-project2-fastslam-specification}

The baseline is the same filter as @sec-slam-fastslam-algorithm, on real data. In every particle, for every scan:

**Association with two gates** (@sec-slam-association-landmark-birth). For each observation $a$ and landmark $j$, compute the innovation $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{aj} = \mathbf{z}_a - h(\mathbf{x}^{[i]}, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j)$ with the bearing wrapped into $[-\pi, \pi)$, $\mathbf{S}_{aj} = \mathbf{H}_\ell\mathbf{P}_{\ell,j}\mathbf{H}_\ell^T + \mathbf{R}$, and $d^2_{aj} = \boldsymbol{\nu}_{aj}^T\mathbf{S}_{aj}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu}_{aj}$ (with a linear solve, never an explicit inverse). Match pairs with $d^2 < \chi^2_{2,0.95} = 5.99$, greedily in order of increasing $d^2$, so that no landmark absorbs two observations from the same scan. An unmatched observation spawns a *tentative* landmark only if $d^2 > \chi^2_{2,0.999} = 13.82$ for every landmark in the particle; otherwise it is ambiguous and discarded. Joint compatibility (@sec-slam-association-joint-compatibility) is a worthwhile extension where trees stand close together.

**Weights** (@sec-slam-landmark-weighting). A matched observation contributes its Gaussian likelihood,

$$
\log w^{[i]} \leftarrow \log w^{[i]} - \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol{\nu}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu} - \tfrac12\log\det(2\pi\mathbf{S}),
$$

and a new or discarded observation contributes the constant $\log p_0$, the density of a measurement that the particle's map does not explain [@Montemerlo2003FastSLAM2; @ProbRob]. Every observation thus contributes exactly one factor to every particle. The default `FastSLAM.log_p0` treats such a measurement as uniform over the sensor footprint, $p_0 = 1/(r_{\max}\,\pi) = 1/(75\pi)\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{rad}^{-1}$. Skipping $p_0$ compares densities against an implicit 1 per (m rad), and whether that rewards or punishes inventing trees depends on your units.

**Landmark management.** A tentative landmark becomes confirmed after three successful associations (`confirm_associations`); a tentative landmark not seen for `tentative_timeout_s` (2 s by default, about nine scans) is deleted. Confirmed landmarks stay.

**Normalization and resampling.** Keep weights in log space and normalize with log-sum-exp (`normalize_log_weights`). Resample with systematic resampling (`systematic_resample_indices`, which clamps the last cumulative weight to exactly 1) when $N_\text{eff} = 1/\sum_i (w^{[i]})^2$ drops below $N/2$ (`resample_threshold`).

All thresholds are fields of `FastSLAM` (`gate_threshold`, `birth_threshold`, `new_landmark_log_likelihood`, `resample_threshold`, ...) and of its `motion` and `measurement` configs, and `rng` is its only source of randomness. Change them if you can justify it, and report the values you used.

## Part A: Dataset, Vehicle Model, and Laser Front End {#sec-project2-part-dataset-loading}

**Goal.** Turn the raw log into trustworthy inputs: decoded scans in the right frame, controls turned into laser motion, and tree observations.

1.  Load the data and explain the decoding: the 13-bit mask, the no-return threshold, and what fraction of beams carry no return. Plot several scans in the vehicle frame and confirm the bearing convention with a feature whose side you can tell (for example a tree that drifts from ahead to the left during a left turn).
2.  Reproduce the dead-reckoning comparison that `run_all` prints (`dead_reckoning_comparison`: with and without the encoder correction and the lever arm) and explain the size of each effect. Then show the lever arm where GPS cannot: project tree detections along dead reckoning in a turn and compare how tightly re-observed trees cluster with and without it.
3.  Implement `extract_tree_landmarks`. @sec-mapping-from-laser-scan describes the original detector (`detectTreesI16.m`), whose parameters are collected in `TreeExtractorConfig`; reproduce it, improve it, or replace it, but document every threshold and its reason.
4.  Characterize the front end: detections per scan, the diameter histogram, an overlay of detections on scans, and the effect of at least two extractor thresholds.
5.  Explain your time-synchronization model (@sec-project2-time-synchronization).

A detector that works on one frame and floods the rest of the log with false trees is not a working detector. Neither is one that finds nothing near the hedges where the vehicle turns.

## Part B: Data Association and Landmark Management {#sec-project2-part-b-data}

**Goal.** Decide, in every particle, whether each observation is an existing tree, a new tree, or something to leave alone.

Implement `LandmarkEKF.initialize`, `innovation`, and `updated` (with the Joseph-form covariance update) and `FastSLAM.associate` as specified in @sec-project2-fastslam-specification. Different particles may and should make different decisions; never force one association table onto every particle (@sec-slam-association-per-particle-association). Report matched, new, and discarded observations per scan, the confirmed landmark count against distance travelled, how often tentative landmarks die, and any duplicates you can find near revisited areas.

## Part C: FastSLAM Backend {#sec-project2-part-c-fastslam}

**Goal.** A complete FastSLAM 1.0 on the Victoria Park log.

Implement `FastSLAM.predict` (vectorized over particles, with the encoder correction and the lever arm), `update` (the weights, landmark updates, birth, confirmation, deletion, trajectory bookkeeping, log-sum-exp normalization, and the resampling decision), and `resample`. Each particle holds its laser pose, its trajectory, its landmark dictionary, and a log weight. Use `np.linalg.solve` rather than matrix inverses, wrap every bearing residual, and fill `slam.history` with one record per scan (for example matched, new, and discarded counts, $N_\text{eff}$ before resampling, and whether you resampled) so `run_all` can report it.

Required figures: the estimated trajectory and confirmed map over GPS (aligned), the error against GPS over time next to dead reckoning, $N_\text{eff}$ over time, landmark counts over time, runtime per scan, and one plot of particle behavior (the particle cloud at a few instants, or trajectory spread before and after a revisit).

## Optional Extension: FastSLAM 2.0 {#sec-project2-optional-extension-fastslam}

FastSLAM 2.0 samples each pose from a proposal that already includes the current measurements (@sec-slam-fastslam2), so it needs fewer particles when the laser is much more precise than the odometry, which is the situation here. It is also easier to get subtly wrong: it needs the pose Jacobian (`range_bearing_pose_jacobian` is provided), a per-particle EKF step on the pose, and a different weight. If you implement it, identify the proposal distribution, explain how the observations shape the pose sample, keep the landmark EKFs and diagnostics unchanged, and compare against your FastSLAM 1.0 baseline at equal runtime. It is not required for full credit.

## Part D: Evaluation and Analysis {#sec-project2-part-d-analysis}

**Goal.** Show what your system does, where it fails, and why.

Evaluate with the protocol of @sec-project2-evaluation-protocol. On the first 2000 scans (about 430 s and 1.1 km), the following sensitivity studies are **required**: particle count, gate threshold, and $\mathbf{Q}_u$, which `run_all --sweep particles gate q_scale` runs with the values in its `SWEEPS` table (particles `(10, 25, 50, 100)`, gate `(4.61, 5.99, 9.21)`, $\mathbf{Q}_u$ scaled by `(0.25, 1.0, 4.0)`). Report RMSE, runtime per scan, and the final confirmed landmark count for each, and explain the trends. A particle filter is a random algorithm, so a single run proves little; say how many seeds you ran.

The full run (all 7249 scans), sweeps over other parameters ($\mathbf{R}$, $p_0$, the resampling threshold, extractor thresholds), and results over several seeds are what separate Excellent from Acceptable.

Finally, compare EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, and GraphSLAM for this dataset (state representation, computational scaling, data association, loop closure, suitability, implementation risk), using your own results where you can. You are not required to implement loop closure or pose-graph optimization, but discuss whether your map shows revisits, duplicate trees, or particle depletion around long loops, and what a graph back end and a loop-closure front end would add (@sec-loop-closure).

## Evaluation Protocol {#sec-project2-evaluation-protocol}

Everyone measures the same way, so results can be compared. `victoria_park_slam.evaluation` implements each step and `run_all` applies them.

1.  **Valid GPS fixes** (`valid_gps_mask`). The fixes are cut into runs at gaps longer than 1 s and at jumps, where consecutive fixes are more than 5 m farther apart than the vehicle drove between them (odometry path length). Runs of fewer than five fixes and fixes outside the odometry time span are dropped. GPS is never interpolated across a gap.
2.  **Interpolate the estimate** to the valid fix times. The estimate is the laser track (the weighted-mean particle pose after each update, or the highest-weight particle's path; say which), which is where the antenna is.
3.  **Align** the whole evaluated segment to GPS with one rigid SE(2) transform (`align_se2`: Kabsch/Umeyama, no scale). The alignment removes the arbitrary start frame; it cannot straighten a bent trajectory.
4.  **Report** the position RMSE after alignment, the maximum error, and the error against time.
5.  **Baseline.** Report dead reckoning (with both corrections) over the same fixes, aligned the same way (`dead_reckoning_comparison`).
6.  **Cost and map growth.** Report runtime per scan (mean and maximum of predict plus update, on stated hardware) and the landmark count (all and confirmed, highest-weight particle) against scan index or distance. A map that grows with every scan rather than with explored area is a symptom, not a feature.

For orientation: over the first 2000 scans, dead reckoning with both corrections has an RMSE of about 32 m against GPS, and a sound FastSLAM 1.0 brings that down to a few meters. Over the full run, dead reckoning drifts to about 93 m RMSE. GPS itself is good to a meter or two where it is valid, so do not chase centimeters.

## Deliverables {#sec-project2-deliverables}

Submit (@sec-project2-logistics):

1.  The code archive: your `victoria_park_slam` package with the deliverables implemented, any scripts or notebooks, and a `README` with the commands that regenerate every figure and table.
2.  Tests or validation scripts for the parts you added beyond the provided tests (for example a test of your extractor on a hand-made scan, or of any Jacobian you derived).
3.  The report PDF, with: the dataset conventions you verified and how; the vehicle, lever-arm, and timing model with parameter values; the observation model and the landmark EKF; the front end and its characterization; the association and landmark-management design; the FastSLAM implementation and all tuning values ($\mathbf{Q}_u$, $\mathbf{R}$, gates, $p_0$, particle count, resampling threshold, seeds); the evaluation of @sec-project2-evaluation-protocol with the required figures and sweeps; the method comparison; and a failure-mode discussion.

Keep the report concise and technical. Show evidence. Do not write a travel essay about the park unless it somehow explains a covariance matrix.

## Suggested Milestones {#sec-project2-suggested-milestones}

1.  Load the data, plot scans in the vehicle frame, and reproduce the dead-reckoning comparison.
2.  Build the tree extractor on a few hundred scans, then check it on the whole log.
3.  Implement the landmark EKF and pass its tests; check any Jacobian you add with `numerical_jacobian`.
4.  Implement prediction, association, update, and resampling; pass the synthetic-loop test.
5.  Run the first 2000 scans with `run_all`, read the diagnostics, and tune.
6.  Run the required sweeps, then (for Excellent) the full log and the extra studies.
7.  Write the report around the evidence.
